claim: A rotary's acceleration byte is read through its top four bits, and the sixteen entries that leaves are what the rotor's loop multiplies the difference by before shifting it. So the distance the rotor stops short of the rate entry it was aimed at is one constant divided by what the entry holds. What the entries hold is a sequence: the first ten count up, one through ten, and then they double -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight. 14 of the sixteen are readable and 12 of those land on that sequence inside what their own take told a rate apart to, with one constant over the whole table and nothing else fitted. The last one does not: it reads 168 where the doubling says 256, five times what the take resolves, and it is published as the number it is. The byte is not a shift count, which is what a four-bit acceleration invited: the distance does not halve per step of it, and the near-four between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults happen to sit in this table. The two rotors are one routine reached twice -- at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent. And the constant, 0.9768 Hz, names the clock a fifth time by a route none of the other four used: it is a rate divided by a power of two, and at thirty-two kilohertz that power is 14.9996 while at forty-four and forty-eight no integer power comes within four tenths.
named: a four-bit acceleration that multiplies the difference before the shift

What the unit holds at the entry the run below aimed at, read by sending the rotor down onto it from the top of the table rather than up to it. The two descents are at accelerations five entries apart and return the same number, which is what says a descent arrives and carries no acceleration in the reading. The third row climbed to the same entry and is the tie to the sweep: the distance it leaves is the distance the same byte gave aimed twelve times higher.

The same descent onto a second entry, a fifth of the way up the table rather than near the bottom of it, which is the entry the middle sweep aimed at. Its climb row is the third reading of one distance at three aims twelve times apart, which is what says the distance does not depend on where the rotor was sent -- it is the same number to a ten-thousandth of a hertz at all three.

The top of the byte read with the rotor aimed at an entry twelve times slower than the first sweep used and the note held a minute rather than eight seconds. A take pins a rate to a fraction of the rate, so the same distance in hertz stands an order further above what the take tells apart here, and the entries whose distance is thousandths of a hertz are readable rather than bounded.

The top entry taken again after thirty seconds instead of ten. Where waiting longer changes nothing the two takes are a repeat of one setting, and at the entry that arrives fastest that is what they are for: they come back 0.0001 Hz apart, which is what the reading is worth where the distance being measured is under six thousandths.

document_rows.why: Which byte is which, and the width of what it holds. The page prints a range of sixteen values against an address that accepts a hundred and twenty-eight, which is a statement about the page; that the unit reaches those sixteen by the byte's top four bits is read off the boundary pairs below and is not on the page.

era_priors.claim: A control processor of this period closes a lag with a subtract, a shift and an add, and the only cheap place to put a per-parameter amount in it is a multiply of the difference before the shift. A multiply by a small integer is a shift and an add or two; a divide is neither.
era_priors.why: It is what makes a distance of one constant over a small integer the thing to look for rather than a distance halving per step, and the records say which of the two it is.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The multiplier had turned out to be a power of two per step, which is the reading this claim replaces.

adds: The records say what each rotor turned at, at each setting of the byte the page calls its acceleration, with the other rotor silenced and the rate byte held. What is read out of them here is that the byte is taken by its top four bits, that the sixteen entries are a multiplier rather than a shift count, what that multiplier is over the first ten of them, what the constant is, and that the constant is a clock over a power of two. The records name no bits, no multiplier and no clock, and say so.

what_the_table_holds.what: One number per entry, as the distance the rotor stops short by and as the multiplier that is its reciprocal, against the sequence rather than against a line. Which of the two the distance was taken against -- a number the unit stated or this project's reading of the rate table -- is carried beside each entry, because that is what the departures are made of.

and_how_many_sit_inside_what_their_own_t.what: The bar is per entry and it is the record's own. A percentage will not do here: the distances run from three tenths of a hertz to five thousandths, so one per cent is two orders apart between the ends of the table, and the takes that read them differ by an order in what they tell a rate apart to.

and_where_the_departures_come_from.what: An entry read against a number the unit stated lands on the sequence far closer than one read against a curve this project fitted, and the difference between the two is the size of the rate table's own error rather than of anything the acceleration byte does.
and_where_the_departures_come_from.and_what_would_close_it: Descending onto the entries the other runs aimed at, the same way this one was read. The top of the rate table cannot be descended onto because nothing is above it, so those entries keep the table's error whatever is done.

the_entry_that_is_not_on_it.how_far_out_it_is: The distance the doubling asks for is 0.00382 Hz and the reading is 0.00580, which is 5 times what that take told a rate apart to. Read the other way, the multiplier is 168 give or take 12, and the sequence's next number is outside that by a wide margin.
the_entry_that_is_not_on_it.and_it_is_not_the_rate_table: This entry's distance was taken against a number the unit stated, so it carries none of the table error the entries above do -- both the reading and what it is subtracted from come off the same evening and the same held block, so a reading bias cancels between them.

how_the_byte_is_read.what: Four bits, and the readings that say so are the settings that share an entry. This is a property and not a residual: a byte taken whole puts two settings of one run of eight between eight and seven hundred per cent apart, and the records put them inside a per cent.
how_the_byte_is_read.why_the_first_of_those_still_counts: Entry 0 is refused as a distance -- the rotor is still climbing there at ten seconds and at forty-five -- and its five settings still agree with each other to a quarter of a per cent. A rotor still on its way tells you nothing about where it stops and everything about whether those five settings are one number.

and_the_two_rotors_are_one_routine.what: The rate claim beside this one reads two distances, 0.245 Hz on the low rotor and 0.062 on the high, and both runs that measured them left this byte at the unit's own defaults -- 24 and 88. Moving the byte says the four to one is the two defaults.
and_the_two_rotors_are_one_routine.and_where_their_defaults_sit: 24 is entry 3 and 88 is entry 11. Entry 3 is on the line and entry 11 is well off it, so the ratio between them is 3.96 rather than the three the line would give -- which is why it landed near four and why reading that as two powers of two was reading a coincidence.

and_the_constant_is_a_clock_over_a_power.what: The constant is 0.9768 Hz, read off the two entries whose distance was taken against a number the unit itself stated rather than against a curve fitted here. A distance in hertz divided by a sample rate is a pure number, and what this one is at thirty-two kilohertz is a power of two.
and_the_constant_is_a_clock_over_a_power.and_it_sharpened_when_the_entry_was_meas: Round one read this constant against entries of the rate table this project had fitted, and it came out 0.79 per cent from a whole power. Read against the one entry the unit was asked for directly it is inside a tenth of that. Nothing about the candidate changed between the two -- what changed is what the distance was subtracted from.
and_the_constant_is_a_clock_over_a_power.why_this_is_a_reading_and_not_a_coincide: The rate was not chosen here. Four other structures in this archive name thirty-two kilohertz before this one, each by a different route, so what is being asked is whether a fifth quantity agrees with a number already fixed -- not which number makes this quantity tidy. What it would take to be wrong is stated: at the two other rates a part of this period could have run at, the nearest integer power of two is four tenths of a power away in both directions.
and_the_constant_is_a_clock_over_a_power.and_what_it_does_not_say: Which power, in the sense of how the rotor's rate is stored. A stopping distance of one part in two to the fifteen of the sample rate is what is measured; whether that is a seventeen-bit shift of a thirty-two-bit phase increment or a nine-bit shift of a twenty-four-bit one is the same reading, and nothing here separates them.

alternatives.reading: The entry is a shift count, so the distance halves at every step of it -- which is what a four-bit acceleration invites and what the rate claim beside this one read into the four to one between the two rotors.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The shape of the table. Scored through the same gates it is 0.01475 octaves against the winner's 0.00046, and it fails where its own structure lives: a halving per step is a factor of thirty-two over the five entries between the two rotors' defaults, and the records put them a factor of four apart.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier is taken from the whole byte rather than from its top four bits.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: A property, not a residual -- on the median it is 0.00219 against 0.00046 and that is not what decides it. Four runs of eight were read at two settings each, and the distances inside them agree to between 0.02 and 0.67 per cent. A whole byte puts the same pairs between 7.9 and 700.0 per cent apart.

alternatives.reading: The byte does not set the distance at all, and the two rotors' distances differ because the rotors do.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The sweep. The distance runs from 0.9728 Hz to 0.0029 Hz across the byte, a factor of 335, and the low rotor set to the high rotor's default returns the high rotor's distance.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier above the tenth entry is a law of its own rather than four numbers -- the table's top half on a different footing from its bottom half, which is what a hand-made table looks like and also what a second formula looks like.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The run it queued, once the entry the rotor was aimed at had been measured rather than fitted. It is a law and not four numbers: above the tenth entry the table doubles -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight -- and four of those five land inside what their own take told a rate apart to. Scored against the same records with the same single constant, the sequence is worst by 0.00356 octaves on the low rotor where the line is worst by 0.10174, which is the same comparison round one made and the first time the top of the table has been in it. The sixteenth entry is not on the sequence and is published as the number it is.

alternatives.reading: The sixteenth entry is on the doubling after all, and what is read there is the rate table's own error at the entry the rotor was aimed at rather than a distance the byte set.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The entry it was aimed at was measured, not fitted. The descent and the climb are two takes of the same evening on the same held block, so the distance between them is a difference of two readings of one quantity and a reading bias cancels in it. What is left is 0.00580 Hz against the 0.00382 the doubling asks for, and against 0.00040 Hz that the take told a rate apart to.

alternatives.reading: The entries between the tenth and the sixteenth are on whole numbers other than these -- the departures being real rather than a reading.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The bar the departures are read against, which is per entry and is the record's own. A distance is a number of hertz and the takes here tell a rate apart to between two ten-thousandths and nine thousandths of one, so the question is not how many per cent an entry is off: it is whether the reading can tell it from the sequence. 12 of 14 cannot. The two that can are entries [7, 15] -- one at 1.2 times its take's own spread, which is the bar and not a margin over it, and the last entry, which is dealt with above. Two of the entries also had the number they were subtracted from measured after this was queued, and the one that moved most moved onto its whole number: the eleventh entry read 1.7 per cent off sixteen against a fitted aim and 0.1 per cent off it against one the unit stated.

and_the_two_constants.what: One constant is fitted per rotor and they come back 0.977 Hz and 0.934. The low rotor's is read against an entry the unit stated and the high rotor's is not -- nothing has been descended onto on that rotor's rate byte -- and the high rotor's distances are four times smaller, so the same table error is four times more of them. The difference between the two constants is what that costs, and it is not evidence that the rotors differ.

which_readings_were_admitted.why: Decided by the records and before any candidate saw them. A reading is refused if the rotor was still climbing at the entry it was set to, which the settings taken at two settle times say, or if the distance does not stand ten times over what that take told a rate apart to. The bar is per take rather than one number for all of them: the runs behind this table aimed a rotor at ten hertz, at two and at less than one, and a take pins a rate to a fraction of the rate, so one floor over all of them is an order too coarse at one end.

gross.why: median 0.00046 octaves on the low rotor against the 2.3554 octaves this byte commands, and 0.00069 against 0.0319 on the high rotor, with one constant fitted per rotor and the two constants coming out at 0.98 and 0.999 Hz.

properties.why: Two properties, and neither is a residual. Settings that share an entry return one distance, to within a per cent on four runs of eight. And the two rotors return the same table: at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, which is what says the four to one between their defaults is the two defaults.

power.why: The shift count is beaten on the residual by a factor of 32 and the whole byte is beaten by a property it contradicts rather than by its residual, which is the stronger of the two. The byte doing nothing is in the ranking because both records that closed the rate claim had to assume it.

breakdown.why: The winner's worst is 0.03882 octaves at setting 104, against 0.00013 of floor -- which is a lean and is reported rather than explained away.
breakdown.read_as: It is the top of the byte and it is one-sided. From entry 10 up the multiplier runs above the line at every entry and by more at each, so the model reads the rotor as further from its target than it was. That is the alternative left standing and it carries the run that would settle it. Below that entry the residual is inside what the run resolves at every admitted setting of both rotors.

refuted_by: Two settings inside one run of eight returning different distances, which would take the four bits away. Or the two rotors returning different distances at one setting of the byte, which would make them two routines and put the four to one back on the rotors. Or the constant turning out to depend on the entry the rotor was aimed at, which would make it a ratio rather than a distance -- the same entry has now been read aimed at 10.00 Hz and at 0.8488, twelve times apart, and the two distances differ by 0.0001 Hz. Or an entry of the sequence moving off its whole number as the entry it was aimed at is measured rather than fitted, which is what the standing alternative asks.
what_this_does_not_settle: How long the rotor takes. Every take here waited ten seconds or forty-five and then held a note, so what is measured is where the rotor stopped and never the path. The bottom two entries are refused for exactly that: the rotor is still climbing at both settle times, so what they would say about the distance is a reading of the wait. A take begun before the write would say something about the path and none was made.

Whether the fast rate bytes are aimed the same way. This byte is printed against a rotor and not against one of its two rates, so one acceleration for both is the thing to expect -- but the fast rate bytes have no reading at all yet, because the speed switch was never switched.

What the multiplier is in the part's own units. The constant is a distance in hertz and the entries are its reciprocal scaled by it, so what is measured is a ratio between entries and one absolute number. Whether the stored entry is the position plus one or that times something is not readable from the output.

What the sixteenth entry holds. It reads 168 give or take 12, which is 5 times what the take resolves away from where the doubling puts it -- so what is published there is a number and not a place in the sequence, and nothing here says why one entry of sixteen would leave a pattern the other fifteen keep. Nor is it queueable: aiming the rotor at the slowest entry it can climb to would halve what the take resolves and leave the multiplier good to about six, where the whole numbers it is being chosen between are one apart.

Whether the first two entries are on the sequence. They are refused because the rotor is still climbing at both settle times, and a take begun before the write would be needed to say anything about them -- which is a reading of the path and this run measures only where the rotor stopped.

and_the_rate_table_is_a_thousandth_over_.what: A rotor sent down onto an entry arrives on it, because falling the shift floors -- which is measured on this type at another entry and is the closed rate claim's own central reading. So a descent reads the unit's value for an entry with no acceleration in it at all, and this run made two.
and_the_rate_table_is_a_thousandth_over_.how_it_was_checked: Two descents, at acceleration bytes 24 and 120 -- five entries apart in the table this claim is about, and a factor of forty apart in how hard the rotor was pulled. They returned the same rate to four decimals, which is what says the descent arrives and that the number is the entry rather than a second stopping distance.
and_the_rate_table_is_a_thousandth_over_.and_what_it_does_to_the_claim_beside_thi: Nothing that refutes it. The rate claim's own residual is larger than this difference, so the table stands where it stood; what is new is that one of its entries now has a number the unit stated beside the number that was fitted, and they differ by less than the claim's worst case. Reading the rest of that table the same way is a run and is queued there.
